title: Pakistan's Space Push With China's Help Must Shape India's Planning, Says CDS
excerpt: General N S Raja Subramani told a New Delhi seminar that Chinese ISR, navigation and timing capabilities will be available to Pakistan, and pointed to the SBS-3 surveillance programme as India's answer.
body:
• Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani said Pakistan's space capability is improving with Chinese help, and Turkey's assistance should also be taken for granted.
  • Whatever capabilities China has in intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), positioning, navigation and timing will be available to Pakistan, he said—and India must factor that into its planning.
  • India's response rests on the Space-Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-3) programme, more satellites built and launched with private-sector help, and shorter revisit times over its borders rather than matching China system for system.
  • The CDS also warned that India is already being subjected to cognitive warfare aimed at sowing division and weakening national morale.

India's top military officer has put military space at the centre of the country's security planning, warning that Pakistan's space capabilities are improving with Chinese assistance and that India must plan on the basis that Chinese space-based capabilities will be available to Islamabad in a crisis.

Speaking at the Vivekananda International Foundation in New Delhi on Friday, at a session on the future of warfare and India's preparedness to conduct multi-domain operations, Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani said Pakistan's space agency SUPARCO was also working to develop its own capability, and that Turkish help for Pakistan should be assumed. The session was moderated by former CDS General Anil Chauhan, who held the post during Operation Sindoor.

"Whatever capabilities are available with the Chinese in terms of ISR, positional navigation, timing, etc., will be available to the Pakistanis, so that we will have to factor into our calculus. Their ISR will be better."

— General N S Raja Subramani, Chief of Defence Staff

Why the space remarks matter

The comments came in response to a question about China's Shenzhou-24 crewed mission, which carried Pakistani national Muhammad Zeeshan Ali — the first foreign citizen to take part in China's crewed space programme, according to reports of the event. For the CDS, the significance was not the flight itself but what growing China-Pakistan space cooperation means for India's surveillance problem: better Pakistani access to satellite imagery, communications and positioning services that shape outcomes in conventional and hybrid conflict.

General Subramani said the distinction between war and peace is increasingly blurred, with competition in cyber, space, electronic and cognitive domains running before, during and after open fighting. "Even today, we are being subjected to cognitive warfare by our adversaries in an insidious manner, to sow seeds of division in society, create internal rifts, weaken the will and morale of the nation," he said, linking the campaign to deepfakes, artificial intelligence and social media manipulation.

India's answer: SBS-3 and more satellites

The CDS pointed to the Space-Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-3) programme as the centrepiece of India's response. "When Space-Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-3) comes in, it will enhance our capability to a great extent," he said. He added that India is working on ways to build and launch more satellites, with greater participation from private companies and entrepreneurs.

He was explicit that India would not try to match China piece for piece. India needs enough capability to watch its borders and reduce revisit time — the gap between satellite passes over the same area — rather than replicate every Chinese system, he said. He also cautioned that technological superiority is "only transitory" and has to be renewed constantly, and described a battlefield made transparent by persistent surveillance, in which, as he put it, anybody who is seen will be fixed and killed.

What to watch

The remarks set the terms for India's military space build-up: SBS-3's progress, the pace of military satellite launches, and how much of that work goes to private industry. They also signal that Indian planning will formally assume a combined China-Pakistan capability in ISR and navigation in any future crisis — a planning assumption that will shape procurement and posture on both the northern and western frontiers.
